iut_type: Post-launch running-change strategy -- shipping a product without Bluetooth certification initially, then adding and certifying Bluetooth support later via a firmware update before marketing it as Bluetooth-compatible
customer_question: Is it acceptable, under Bluetooth's rules, to launch our product without Bluetooth support first, then later perform a running change (post-launch software revision) to add Bluetooth functionality, get it certified at that point, and only then market the product as Bluetooth-compatible?
question_variants: What specifically triggers the need for a new Bluetooth registration when a software update is released?
Can a software-only update that doesn't add new Bluetooth functionality skip re-registration?
actual_issue: The customer realized that an uncertified Bluetooth host stack (open-source BlueZ via AMD's Petalinux SDK) would not realistically meet their product's mass-production launch schedule, given the minimum 3-month lead time and BlueZ's historically low first-pass certification rate, and wanted to know whether they could instead launch the product without Bluetooth support and add/certify it later via a post-launch firmware update.
plain_english_explanation: A new Bluetooth registration is required whenever a software change adds at least one newly-supported item to the ICS (functionality-definition) table of any layer defined in the Bluetooth Core Specification or a Profile Specification. Conversely, a software fix or revision that does NOT add any new ICS-supported item does not require a new registration. This means a manufacturer can legitimately launch a product without Bluetooth support initially, and later perform a running change that adds Bluetooth functionality via a firmware update -- triggering the need for a new registration at that point (since this is a genuine addition of new ICS-supported functionality). Marketing, PR, sales claims, exhibition, or press releases describing the product as Bluetooth-compatible can only begin once that registration is completed and the listing becomes visible to third parties -- not before. This running-change approach is a legitimate way to decouple a product's initial launch schedule from the Bluetooth certification timeline when an uncertified host stack's testing timeline is too unpredictable to meet the production schedule.
consultant_answer: Yes, this is acceptable: a new registration is only triggered when a software change adds at least one newly-supported ICS item to any Core Specification or Profile Specification layer -- a change that doesn't add new ICS-supported functionality doesn't need re-registration. So you can launch without Bluetooth support now, and later perform a running change that adds Bluetooth via firmware update, registering and certifying it at that point. Just keep in mind you can only start marketing the product as Bluetooth-compatible once that registration is completed and publicly visible, not before.
decision_logic: When a customer's uncertified Bluetooth implementation timeline doesn't fit their product's launch schedule, offer the running-change strategy as a legitimate alternative: launch without Bluetooth support, add and certify it later via a firmware update (which triggers new registration only because it adds new ICS-supported functionality), and begin Bluetooth-compatible marketing claims only once that later registration is complete and publicly visible.
final_recommendation: When a customer's certification timeline conflicts with their production schedule, proactively offer the running-change strategy (launch without the feature, add and certify it later) as a legitimate decoupling option, while being clear that the underlying ICS-table-support-addition rule is what triggers the later registration requirement.
risk_if_done_wrong: A customer who isn't aware that ICS-supported functionality additions specifically trigger new registration requirements (rather than any software update in general) might either over-register for inconsequential changes or under-register when a meaningful feature addition actually requires it; marketing Bluetooth compatibility before the later registration is publicly visible would violate SIG's disclosure timing requirement.
